entities.summary:
The Battle of Warsaw, fought from August 13 to 25, 1920, was a pivotal event in the Polish-Soviet War. It was a decisive victory for the Polish Army, led by General Władysław Sikorski, which halted the Soviet Red Army's advance on Warsaw.

The battle was a turning point in the war, as it prevented the Soviet Union from capturing the Polish capital and forced them to retreat from the city. The Polish Army's success was largely due to the bravery and cunning of its soldiers, who used innovative tactics to outmaneuver the Soviets. The battle also marked a significant shift in the war's momentum, as the Polish Army began to gain the upper hand.

The legacy of the Battle of Warsaw can be seen in the subsequent Polish-Soviet Treaty of Riga, which established the modern borders of Poland and led to the country's recognition as an independent state. The battle also had a lasting impact on Polish national identity, as it cemented the country's reputation as a fierce defender of its sovereignty. 'The Polish people will never forget the sacrifices made by our soldiers at Warsaw, for they fought not only for their country, but for the freedom of all nations.' General Władysław Sikorski.

In the end, the Battle of Warsaw was a testament to the strength and resilience of the Polish people, who had fought against overwhelming odds to preserve their nation's independence.
